ZURICH, Oct 20 : ABB is continuing to see a boom in spending on data centres used to power artificial intelligence, the engineering group said on Tuesday, as it reported its latest earnings. The Swiss company said its operational earnings before interest, tax and amortisation jumped 24 per cent to $2.03 billion in the three months to the end of September, slightly ahead of analyst forecasts for $2.0 billion. Revenue meanwhile rose 14 per cent to $9.70 billion, slightly below forecasts of $9.74 billion in a company gathered consensus. ABB, which makes electrification and automation products used by factories, ships and ports, has been seeing strong demand for products like power distribution and cooling systems used in data centres. A surge in spending on AI and data centres is propping up the global economy, helping it withstand the energy shock from the Middle East war, the IMF said last week, although it said a reassessment of efficiency gains from adopting the technology could dent investment. During the third quarter ABB said it had seen a triple digit increase in orders for data centre products, continuing the trend it saw during the second quarter.

SINGAPORE: Singapore-headquartered tech conglomerate Sea Limited is planning a public listing for its financial services arm Monee and will also launch an AI enterprise platform business, according to an internal memo sent on Tuesday (Oct 20). Founder Forrest Li, in a memo to employees that was reviewed by Reuters, said he believed going public would give its financial payments and services business the "resources and the room to go further and faster than it can today”.  The business operates in Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Brazil and offers mobile wallets, payments processing, credit and banking services. Sea did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The memo said the tech group would also launch an AI-first enterprise platform named Sea Cloud.  In the memo, which was sent on the ninth anniversary of the group’s public listing in New York, Li said the quarterly revenue for the group had grown more than 80 times over that period to US$7.8 billion.

LONDON, Oct 20 : Demand for safe-haven assets is strong as AI jitters hurt tech stocks, the Iran war continues and keeps energy prices elevated, while worries about high government debt loads persist. Yet traditional safe havens have not performed as well as expected this year: Gold sold off after the start of the Iran war as investors ditched top-performing assets given losses elsewhere. Government bonds, once considered one of the world's safest assets, are volatile. Here is a look at how some safe havens currently stack up. 1) LOVE/HATE RELATIONSHIP WITH THE DOLLAR

Breaking with last year's 'sell US' theme, the dollar has rallied since the Iran war started, up 4 per cent since late February. That has reinforced its role as a go-to safe haven at times of global stress. A strong economy, higher rates, and the US's energy-exporter status have helped. But factors that caused traders to question the dollar's long-term safe-haven status, such as a more than $40 trillion debt pile and policy uncertainty, have not dissipated. The dollar is also vulnerable to tech selling as it has benefited from record capital inflows into US shares on optimism over the AI investment boom. The dollar could be nearing the back end of a bull market, Societe Generale chief FX strategist Kit Juckes said. "It hasn't got that much further to go," he noted, but said it was hard to justify a sustained bet against the dollar at present because the "big global story is that the dollar is a petrocurrency and we're in the middle of an energy crisis". 2) EUROPE WOBBLES, BUY SWISSIE One takeaway from France-driven bond turmoil is that the Swiss franc is a haven of choice when Europe wobbles. It is up over 2 per cent so far this month against the euro, poised for its biggest monthly jump since late 2023. "Concerns about France's public finances and election uncertainty in France and Spain have supported the franc," said Georgette Boele, senior FX & oil strategist at ABN Amro. She added that investors were also becoming less keen to use the franc to fund carry trades, preferring not to position against a currency with safe-haven qualities. Swiss rates at 0 per cent make the franc popular in trades where investors borrow in a currency with low rates to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. The AI jitters should also benefit the Swiss franc, analysts said. 3) GERMAN BONDS A RELATIVE WINNER Government bonds' reputation as a safe haven has been battered by fiscal concerns. Borrowing costs from the US to Japan recently hit multi-decade highs. The tech-driven stocks selloff has, however, renewed some demand for bonds. There is another noticeable development. When US and French 10-year bond yields hit 24-year peaks earlier this month, German yields fell as their prices rose. Investors say that is a clear sign that triple-A rated German Bunds stand out as safe havens among major economies. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said Germany would remain the anchor of stability in Europe amid bond turmoil and was "getting fit" after years of stagnation. "Everyone worries about contagion in Europe and whether the Bund just gets dragged along with (French) OATs, (Italian) BTPs, so it's good that the Bund has acted as that European risk-off instrument," said Johnathan Owen, a portfolio manager at TwentyFour Asset Management. 4) DID YOU FORGET SHORT-DATED BONDS? Overall, high debt among major economies will continue to hurt long-dated bonds' safe-haven status, investors said. But short-dated government bonds provide some shelter because they are less sensitive to debt worries. "We really like short-dated bonds," said Rory McPherson, chief market strategist at Wren Sterling. "Because of all the concerns over debts and deficits, we haven't been buying longer-dated bonds." 5) GOLD KEEPS ITS SPARKLE Gold, another traditional safe haven, has had a bumpy ride. After hitting record highs at $5,595 per troy ounce in January, it fell after the Iran war started as investors tapped the precious metal, given losses elsewhere. Gold rallied again in August as inflation fears and concern that the Federal Reserve was not doing enough to contain price pressures returned. It is trading around $4,175. Central bank buying and safe-haven demand support prices above $4,000, analysts say. While high interest rates should limit gold's upside, a tense geopolitical backdrop and US fiscal worries should bolster the safe-haven metal further out. "In the longer term, gold should again benefit from continued strong central-bank buying and renewed concerns over US debt and its rising interest burden," said Julius Baer analyst Carsten Menke.

TOKYO, Oct 20 : Asian stocks retreated broadly on Tuesday while oil prices rose as geopolitical risks rattled sentiment ahead of key results from AI bellwether companies.  The euro recouped some losses from the previous session that were spurred by escalating riots in France. Crude prices resumed their climb as markets weighed an executive order from US President Donald Trump that waived some sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy. The spotlight is on corporate earnings, with investors seeking fresh evidence that consumers and the broader economy remain resilient. Quarterly earnings are due from SpaceX and Netflix on Tuesday, with results from AI heavyweights such as Meta and Tesla scheduled for later in the week. "The market is happy to cover shorts and unwind defensive trades, but that's very different from having the conviction to rebuild aggressive exposure to AI," Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, said in a note. "French sovereign risk is clearly being priced into European equities, but the euro's resilience suggests traders aren't yet treating it as a systemic European problem."

The MSCI Asia ex-Japan index fell 1.14 per cent, while Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 0.98 per cent. South Korea’s KOSPI tumbled 3.92 per cent. In early European trade, the pan-region Euro Stoxx 50 futures slipped 0.57 per cent, German DAX futures dipped 0.33 per cent and FTSE futures lost 0.47 per cent. US stock futures, the S&P 500 e-minis, rose 0.12 per cent to 7,743.5.   The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, fell 0.16 per cent to 101.80, with the euro up 0.17 per cent at $1.1229. The Japanese yen strengthened 0.16 per cent to 158.24 per dollar, and sterling rose 0.21 per cent to $1.3327. Overnight, French authorities set curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, Lille and Nice, after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests. And in the Middle East, dozens were killed and more than 200 were injured after an attack by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province. EARNINGS AND AI MAJORS IN FOCUS Netflix is expected to report slowing revenue growth in the third quarter, while SpaceX is forecast to report $12.74 billion in quarterly revenue. General Motors, Hasbro, Halliburton, and 3M are among the more established names due to report on Tuesday. Along with quarterly results, markets are increasingly focused on the massive spending plans of the major AI players. Facebook operator Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers expected to increase combined capital expenditure to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. "Investors are fine with AI being used more. What they're questioning is whether every dollar of AI capex earns more than it costs to finance," said Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for APAC at State Street Investment Management. "AI has gone from an earnings story to a balance-sheet story, and now a unit-economics story to some extent." Shares in South Korean AI infrastructure company Elice Group plunged nearly 30 per cent below their initial public offering price in their market debut, after the firm raised 201.1 billion won ($151.12 million) in an IPO. US crude rose 0.18 per cent to $103.85 a barrel and Brent rose to $109.64 per barrel, up 0.08 per cent on the day. Spot gold rose 0.13 per cent to $4,145.25 an ounce.   An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas. However, Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter. Inflationary pressures from elevated oil prices have put most major central banks on a tightening bias, though with a careful eye on whether economies are resilient enough to absorb higher interest rates. Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials, including Chair Kevin Warsh, suggest policymakers are in no rush to hike rates again. The US Census Bureau is due to release September figures, with housing starts expected to rise to 1.305 million from 1.275 million in August, while building permits are seen at 1.395 million compared with 1.403 million.  European Central Bank policymaker Martin Kocher is due to speak later on Tuesday, as well as ECB policymaker and Finnish central bank governor Olli Rehn. Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee member Megan Greene will deliver a speech at the London School of Economics. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin gained 0.22 per cent to $82,117.01, and ether rose 0.63 per cent to $2,413.64.

Shares of fintech firm Mynt, operator of mobile wallet GCash, rose 0.5 per cent in its market debut on Tuesday (Oct 20) after the company raised 60.9 billion pesos (US$966.99 million) in the largest initial public offering on record in the Philippines. The stock opened at 6.63 pesos per share, up from its offer price of 6.60 pesos. The Philippine Stock Exchange index was down 0.2 per cent. Mynt sold 8.03 billion shares at 6.60 pesos each. The exercise of an overallotment option increased the deal size to 60.9 billion pesos from 53 billion pesos. The offering comprised both primary and secondary shares. Proceeds from the sale of new shares will go to the company, while proceeds from the secondary shares will go to existing shareholders, according to the IPO prospectus.

Brent crude futures climbed 55 cents, or 0.50 per cent, to $110.10 a barrel by 0319 GMT, after rising as high as $110.70 a barrel in the previous session to their highest since May 20. The US West Texas Intermediate crude (WTI) contract for November delivery, set to expire on Tuesday, was up 0.24 per cent to $103.91. Strong semiconductor-led growth, a recovery in domestic demand and elevated energy costs are likely to keep underlying price pressures firm. Still, the recent moderation in headline inflation and Governor Shin Hyun Song's call for time to assess the effects of the back-to-back hikes give policymakers room to pause this month rather than deliver a third consecutive increase. So there is still room for the BOK to hike." Beyond inflation and growth, the BOK is also weighing financial-stability risks, particularly developments in housing, household debt and financial markets. NEW YORK, Oct 19 : OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic's expected public market debut in mid-November, in an unusually fast fundraising that could value the ChatGPT maker at over $1.4 trillion, according to two people familiar with the matter. The rapid timetable reflects, in part, a desire to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are increasingly tapping in to a similar investor base, the people said, adding that OpenAI wants to capitalize on its recent revenue growth after launching new models. SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round of about $30 billion, one of the people said.  The acceleration underscores how closely the two AI developers are competing for capital as both pursue trillion-dollar price tags, amid growing concern about rising interest rates, significant volatility in technology stocks and rising scrutiny of AI valuations. OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. OpenAI's funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size, the people said.

Some investors view OpenAI’s financing push as an effort to lock in capital from funds that might otherwise devote more of their resources to Anthropic’s IPO, the people said.  OpenAI and SoftBank declined to comment. Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. TRYING TO HEAD OFF COMPARISONS OpenAI is pitching investors on growth that accelerated after the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, saying it had reached $50 billion in annualized revenue and expecting that figure to rise to $70 billion by year-end, according to one of the people. OpenAI has also cut prices on its cheaper models, which it said has boosted usage, and told investors it can further lower the price of AI models, the person added.  Anthropic's annualized revenue reached roughly $65 billion by July, Reuters previously reported. Its quarterly revenue jumped to $16.8 billion in the third quarter from $11.6 billion in the second quarter this year, it told investors, but slowing month-to-month revenue growth has raised concerns among investors about its valuation. OpenAI is seeking to complete the fundraising before Anthropic’s financial disclosures give investors a fuller picture of its business and invite comparisons between the two companies, one person said.  The disclosures could prompt investors to press OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar for more details about the company’s revenue growth and financial outlook, the person added. OpenAI records revenue on a net basis by subtracting partner shares upfront. It has accused Anthropic of inflating its revenue by counting  the full, gross value of contracts sold through third-party cloud providers. Anthropic told Reuters earlier that it follows established accounting practices. "OpenAI could want to set its own valuation and not have to worry about a comp (comparison)," said Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher, who is not working on the deal and commented on a hypothetical basis. "It's really a two-horse race in terms of being public."  OpenAI was last valued at $852 billion in March this year, after a record-breaking $122 billion funding round, including a commitment from Amazon.com, which agreed to invest up to $50 billion in the lab.  The Financial Times previously reported some details of OpenAI’s potential fundraising.   IPO PLANS HIT BY MARKET JITTERS A number of companies preparing to go public have decided to wait until after Anthropic’s planned IPO, wary of competing for investor demand amid market volatility and a pullback in AI stocks, bankers and investors said. Some late-stage companies are also timing private fundraising rounds to avoid coinciding with Anthropic’s expected debut, the bankers and investors said. Some existing and prospective Anthropic investors have argued for a valuation closer to $1.5 trillion for its market debut — instead of the desired $2 trillion — after the AI startup's third-quarter results fell short of expectations, Reuters reported last week. The reassessment comes amid a choppy market since September, with volatility in oil prices, rising bond yields and growing concerns about AI safety weighing on investor appetite for technology stocks. Investors are also scrutinizing the cost of AI infrastructure, including the debt needed to finance the data centers powering the boom. At the center of the latest concerns is cloud provider CoreWeave, whose shares and debt tumbled last week as investors scrutinized the nearly $50 billion in borrowings used to fund its rapid expansion.  The uncertainty has disrupted what had been expected to be a busy autumn for IPOs, with companies reassessing their listing plans amid market volatility and concerns about valuations. Blackstone-backed AirTrunk REIT, Nvidia-backed Firmus and SoftBank-backed SB Energy have either pulled or paused their listings.  Nuclear services company Holtec cited a "perfect storm," driven mainly by uncertainty around data-center demand, when it pulled its US listing last month. Companies in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, widely viewed as a proxy for AI-related semiconductor demand, have shed $1.6 trillion in less than two weeks, while AI infrastructure companies have come under particular pressure.

In all, the researchers studied 20 bone fragments from this species — 14 from Denisova Cave and 6 from other sites in the broader region. The oldest specimen dated to about 250,000 to 200,000 years ago, and the youngest to about 27,000 years ago. The bones themselves were so fragmentary that their shape alone did not reveal that they belonged to a previously unknown large mammal. But the researchers were able to generate 20 ancient genomes from the bones, and these showed that this was a unique species whose evolutionary lineage diverged from the ancestors of the modern-day yak approximately 400,000 years ago.

"It is unusual, especially to recognize a large mammal species from small, unidentifiable fragments," said evolutionary geneticist Love Dalén of the Centre for Palaeogenetics, a collaboration between Stockholm University and the Swedish Museum of Natural History, senior author of the research published in the journal Current Biology. "I'd say that this is related to the advances in the field of ancient DNA, as genetics is a powerful new layer of information applied to ancient materials," said Alexandre Gilardet, a doctoral student at the Centre for Palaeogenetics and co-lead author of the study, along with Centre for Palaeogenetics postdoctoral researcher Jonas Oppenheimer. Genetic evidence alone is not sufficient to allow for giving a scientific name to a new species, so the researchers are calling this one "Yak X." THE ICE AGE LANDSCAPE Dalén said Yak X lived alongside other bovines including steppe bison and the aurochs, the extinct wild ancestor of today's domesticated cattle. It also shared the Ice Age landscape with woolly mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, horses and large predators such as cave hyenas and brown bears, Dalén said. "I'd expect it to have looked more like a yak than a bison, given its close relationship to modern yaks," Dalén said. Yaks are sturdily built animals with horns, long fur and a hump at the shoulders, looking a bit like a hairy ox. The largest males can weigh as much as a ton. Wild yaks are restricted to higher elevations of the Tibetan Plateau. The Yak X discovery deepens the understanding of the diversity of large Ice Age mammals and adds another species to the long list that disappeared at around the end of that epoch. "Using the long, 200,000-year time span of our sampling, we can see that the species may have undergone a population decline during a period of warming around 120,000 years ago, and went extinct some time after our youngest sample, about 27,000 years ago," Oppenheimer said. The vast Siberian expanse was a grassland ecosystem called the mammoth steppe, known as such for its largest denizens. Most of the region was left uncovered by the immense ice sheets that had blanketed large swathes of North America and Europe. The Yak X lineage diverged from the ancestors of modern yaks around the same time as the evolutionary split that occurred between the ursine lineages that led to today's brown bears and polar bears. THE DENISOVANS It was in Denisova Cave in 2008 that scientists unearthed a finger bone that offered the first evidence of the existence of Denisovans, extinct cousins of Neanderthals and our own species, Homo sapiens. Since then, more remains of Denisovans have been discovered in the cave and in several far-flung parts of Asia. Some modern populations of people, especially those in Melanesia and Papua New Guinea, carry a small percentage of DNA from Denisovans, indicating interbreeding with Homo sapiens before the Denisovans became extinct under circumstances that are not well understood. Denisovans were hunter-gatherers who survived in many different types of environments. The Yak X species might have been among the prey that they hunted. "It seems reasonable that Yak X was on the Denisovan menu," Dalén said.

MUMBAI, Oct 19 : Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance said on Monday that Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, BlackRock and Fidelity were among investors who bid in the anchor book of its record $3.2 billion Jio Platforms IPO, which two sources said drew more than $25 billion in demand. The telecoms, cloud and AI group on Monday opened its record initial public offering to institutional investors who can bid for up to 30 per cent of the offering exclusively earmarked for them, before the issue opens for public subscription on Wednesday.  Jio Platforms allocated shares worth over 81 billion rupees ($853.31 million) to anchor investors, a company filing showed on Monday. State-run insurer Life Insurance Corporation, French lender BNP Paribas, JPMorgan, India's largest private-sector lender HDFC Bank were among the other institutions allotted shares in the IPO anchor book.

NEW YORK, Oct 19 : IT services company DXC Technology is in advanced talks to sell its insurance software and services division to private investment firm Eldridge Industries for about $2.4 billion, according to people familiar with the matter. Eldridge is discussing combining the business with Zinnia, its insurance technology platform that provides software and digital infrastructure to life insurance and annuity providers, the sources said. DXC Technology, Eldridge and Zinnia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
